comparator.name: International Business Administration
comparator.academicYear: 2026-2027 (School of Business and Economics Teaching and Examination Regulations and annual programme schedule, the formally adopted documents for the Fall 2026 intake)
comparator.sourceNotes: The programme is taught in English at VU Amsterdam's School of Business and Economics and carries 180 EC over three years. The complete 180-EC pathway is taken from the formally adopted 2026-2027 SBE bachelor Teaching and Examination Regulations and their annual programme schedule for International Business Administration, cross-checked against the current official programme and curriculum pages. Year 1 consists of ten compulsory 6-EC courses; year 2 of eight compulsory 6-EC courses plus one 6-EC restricted-choice elective in period 4 and one in period 5; year 3 of a mandatory 30-EC international exchange semester, compulsory Ethics (6 EC), two 6-EC courses of one chosen specialization and a 12-EC bachelor's thesis written within that specialization. The compulsory zero-credit components (Mentoring Programme (SAM), the English language test and Research Participation I and II) carry no EC and are therefore outside the 180-EC component list. The 2026-2027 annual programme schedule, which forms part of the adopted regulations, requires every student to choose one of eleven year-3 specializations (Accounting, Digital Business Innovation, Economics, Entrepreneurship, Finance, Financial Management, Strategic Human Resource Management / Leadership and Change Management, Management Consulting, Marketing, Strategy and Organization, Transport and Supply Chain Management), each consisting of one fixed 6-EC course in period 4 and one in period 5, and to write the 12-EC thesis on a topic commensurate with that specialization; the regulations themselves list no separate formal tracks. Because the specialization fixes 24 EC of the pathway and the normalized target is the generic bachelor, one specialization is instantiated: Strategy and Organization, selected under the neutral broad-academic-identity rule (see the route selection record), so the year-3 pathway is Foundations of Strategic Management (period 4), Strategic Management from a Practice Perspective: A Day in the Life of a CEO (period 5) and a bachelor's thesis in strategy and organization. The year-2 elective spaces remain preserved as restricted choice. One discrepancy was found and resolved in favour of the formally adopted source: the interest evidence recorded for this target lists international business law as curriculum content, but in the 2026-2027 schedule International Business Law is one of the six period-4 electives, not a compulsory course, so it is represented inside the restricted-choice elective space rather than as a compulsory component.
components: Economic Principles in a Global Era

Restricted choice: one of the six period-4 options listed in the formally adopted 2026-2027 SBE programme schedule (Global Marketing Innovation, International Business Law, Digital Innovation and Virtual Organizing in a Global Setting, Managing People: A Global Perspective, Sustainable Management of Global Supply Chains, IBA Lab I). The space is preserved as restricted choice rather than instantiated with one option.

Restricted choice: one of the four period-5 options listed in the formally adopted 2026-2027 SBE programme schedule (IBA Lab II, Inclusive Growth and Sustainability, Corporate Finance: A Sustainability Perspective, Accounting, Business and Society). IBA Lab II additionally requires enrolment in IBA Lab I in period 4.

Mandatory international exchange semester at one of more than 150 partner universities on six continents; the credits are earned abroad and the specific course content is not fixed by the VU curriculum.

Strategy and Organization specialization course, period 4 (E_IBK3_FSM, 6 EC, level 300). It examines the classical and contemporary debates of strategic management and requires a real-life strategic case analysis. The course page lists the compulsory IBA courses Organization Theory, Academic Skills, International Strategy and Business Research Methods - Quantitative as recommended background; all four precede it in this pathway.
Strategic Management from a Practice Perspective: A Day in the Life of a CEO

Strategy and Organization specialization course, period 5 (E_IBK3_SMPP, 6 EC, level 300). Students act as an executive board and produce a strategic plan covering context analysis, competitive strategy and business model, and corporate strategy. The course page lists Organization Theory, Academic Skills, International Strategy and Foundations of Strategic Management as recommended background; all precede it in this pathway.

Individual 12-EC thesis (E_IBA3_THESI) on an international business topic within the Strategy and Organization specialization, written as a systematic literature review or an empirical study. Students who have not passed Academic Skills, Business Research Methods - Qualitative and Business Research Methods - Quantitative cannot start it; all three precede it in this pathway, and the two specialization courses are its recommended background.

core: International business administration: how firms are organised, managed and operated across borders
Cross-cultural management: how culture and values shape business behaviour, consumer response and management decisions
Global economics: micro- and macroeconomic principles applied to an integrated world economy
Accounting, corporate finance and financial decision-making
Quantitative and qualitative business research methods, statistics and an integrative empirical research project
People in business and society: organisational behaviour, leadership and the management of diverse teams
International strategy, digital technologies and the responsible use of AI in business
Global supply chains, international trade and the cross-border operating environment
Ethics, corporate social responsibility and sustainability in global business
adjacent: Responsible and sustainable international business: sustainability science, circular production and the governance of sustainability
Consumer behaviour and consumer psychology as the basis of marketing decisions
The societal and cultural context in which firms and markets operate
Public policy, regulation and the political economy of international business
questions: How can a company introduce a product and build consumer trust in an unfamiliar cultural market?
How do different cultures view corporate social responsibility and responsible finance, and how should an international firm act on that?
How can trust and cooperation be built in culturally diverse and virtual international teams?
How do European, Asian and South American business environments differ, and what does that mean for strategy and supply chains?
How should persuasion, branding and marketing communication be used responsibly across cultures?

teaches the micro- and macroeconomic principles the programme's global-economics strand depends on, from consumer and firm theory and market structure to aggregate output, unemployment, inflation and the short-run behaviour of goods and financial markets

delivers the research-design and statistics training the programme requires, covering operationalization, sampling, experimental design, survey and laboratory research and descriptive and inferential statistics up to analysis of variance

sets out the legal systems, constitutional, administrative, criminal, international, property, contract and tort law that a cross-border business curriculum presupposes, and practises them through case law and trial simulations
develops a strategic plan from vision to execution and analyses how digital technology change reshapes strategy, business models and corporate social responsibility

works through virtue ethics, deontology and utilitarianism and applies them to practical questions of equality, poverty and wealth, future generations and climate change, which is the moral-reasoning training behind the programme's compulsory ethics course
teaches the full qualitative research cycle of design, data collection and management, interpretation and dissemination, which is the qualitative business-research method the programme requires
teaches students to comprehend a corporate annual report, to analyse financial statements and to use accounting to trace how economic events affect a business

analyses national income, growth, inflation and unemployment, the effect of fiscal and monetary policy, business cycles, economic crises and international trade, the macroeconomic material behind the programme's economics in a global era
introduces leadership theory with an emphasis on self-awareness, goal-setting and emotional intelligence, the personal-leadership foundation on which the programme's people-in-business strand builds

uses the planetary-boundaries framework to establish what sustainability means and which limits business activity operates within, the substantive content of the programme's compulsory global-sustainability course

examines the legal frameworks governing cross-border trade, contracts, sales of goods and services, intellectual property, foreign investment and digital commerce, and practises identifying legal risk in transnational transactions

analyses how AI changes competitiveness, innovation, labour markets and individual business functions and examines AI governance, bias, privacy and accountability, which is the programme's explicit focus on using AI responsibly and critically in business
analyses consumer decision-making under uncertainty, cognitive limitations and non-egoistic preferences, and then imperfect competition, strategic behaviour, general equilibrium and market efficiency

unpacks what drives consumer behaviour and brand engagement, examines digital and AI-driven marketing and requires students to develop marketing plans and brand strategies, which is the cross-cultural marketing content of the programme

examines motivation, group dynamics, organisational culture, power and decision-making inside organisations, the organisational-behaviour subject the programme teaches as organization theory and managing people

examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global business, cross-border governance, geopolitical strategy and global trade, which is the international operating environment the programme is built around
teaches the multivariate statistical models quantitative business research uses, including linear and logistic regression, analysis of (co)variance, factor analysis and non-parametric tests

develops the practical work with business data that the programme's information-systems and analytics strand requires: cleaning, manipulation and visualisation, non-tabular data including text, and an independent data-analysis project

teaches ordinary least squares, generalised least squares and instrumental-variable estimation with formal hypothesis testing and requires an empirical paper, the advanced quantitative analysis the programme's quantitative research strand leads to
requires students to plan and carry out real market research, analyse the findings and report them, which is the integrative empirical research project the programme places in its second year
develops financial decision-making on real cases: analysing financial data, assessing risk and making investment, budgeting and long-term planning decisions

examines how diverse perspectives and experiences shape leadership and requires students to lead inclusively and adaptively across those differences, the cross-cultural people-management content of the programme

studies social-movement theory and environmental justice through the Environmental Justice Atlas, which is the civil-society pressure and the justice claims that international firms actually answer to when they account for their impact

builds the chemistry and materials knowledge behind sustainability claims and ends in a project analysing greenwashing, which is the evidential discipline corporate sustainability claims have to survive

establishes the drivers and physical impacts of anthropogenic climate change and then its consequences for food production, transport, construction, health and migration, together with climate governance and climate justice

trains argument construction and the rhetorical appeals of logos, pathos and ethos in practice, the foundation of professional persuasive communication in business settings

traces the development of sociology within imperialism and colonial responses and engages the leading theories of modernity, which is what makes the differences between European, Asian and South American business settings analysable rather than anecdotal

examines solidarity, social capital, social trust and the civil and public sphere in contemporary societies, the theoretical account of how trust is produced in a society that a firm entering an unfamiliar market has to work with
runs a full product-development cycle: interviewing potential customers, translating their needs into a product concept, developing a production method and analysing environmental impact and cost

alternatives.label: International business across economics, management, marketing, finance and law
alternatives.concept: The closest feasible UCR response to the VU International Business Administration target: the business-administration core of the external programme rebuilt from UCR's Business & Entrepreneurship cluster, combining business and entrepreneurship foundations, micro- and macroeconomics, accounting and finance, marketing and consumer engagement, strategy and digital transformation, the international business environment and its legal frameworks, organisational behaviour and diversity management, and a quantitative and qualitative research-methods sequence. UCR offers no supply-chain management and no business mathematics course, so those parts of the VU core are not reproduced.
alternatives.labelReason: The completed curriculum contains eight economics, accounting and finance courses, four marketing, strategy and international-business courses, four leadership and organisational-behaviour courses, four methods and data courses and two law courses, so the label names that combination rather than presenting the programme as a management degree or as an economics degree. It deliberately does not claim supply-chain management, which the programme does not contain.
progression: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations, Introduction to Economics and Law, Society & Justice open semester one and Research Methods & Statistics follows in semester two, so both gateway courses precede every course that formally requires them and the legal foundation precedes Transnational Business Law in semester four. Accounting & Corporate Finance precedes Money, Banking & Finance; Introduction to Economics precedes International Macroeconomics, Microeconomics & Behavior and Econometrics; Personal Leadership precedes Psychology of Organizations & Leadership; and Research Methods & Statistics and Statistics & Experimental Methods both precede Econometrics and Market Research. Every formal prerequisite is completed in an earlier semester and every course is offered in the term it is assigned to.

alternatives.label: Responsible international business: sustainability, governance and ethics in cross-border firms
alternatives.concept: A related direction built on the target's own explicit commitment to sustainability, responsible decision-making and corporate responsibility across cultures: it keeps the business, economics, accounting and finance foundations and the international operating environment, and then organises the upper years around what responsible conduct actually requires — sustainability science and circular production, the governance of sustainability, public and behavioural economics, transnational business law, ethics and the civil-society claims firms answer to. Its organising logic is the firm's responsibility for its impact rather than the general administration of the firm.
alternatives.labelReason: Six of the completed courses come from environment and sustainability and two from sociology and public economics, alongside a business, economics, finance, law and organisational core, so the label names responsible international business rather than presenting the programme as a sustainability-science degree or as a general business degree.
progression: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations, Introduction to Economics and Accounting & Corporate Finance open semester one and Research Methods & Statistics follows in semester two, so both gateway courses precede every course that formally requires them. Sustainability Essentials I in semester three precedes Sustainability Essentials II in semester four, which in turn precedes R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation in semester five, satisfying the full environment-cluster chain. Introduction to Economics precedes Public Economics and Behavioral Economics, Accounting & Corporate Finance precedes Money, Banking & Finance, and Law, Society & Justice precedes Transnational Business Law. Every formal prerequisite is completed earlier and every course is available in its assigned term.
alternatives.distinctness: Alternative 1 reproduces the administration of an international firm: it spends its upper years on marketing, market research, econometrics, strategy and digital transformation. Alternative 2 starts from the target's own question about how cultures view corporate social responsibility and responsible finance and answers it with the material that makes responsibility assessable: sustainability science and the evidential discipline of Sustainability Essentials II, lifecycle and circular-production analysis, recycling and remediation, climate change, the governance of sustainability, public economics and social-movement and environmental-justice sociology. The consequence is curricular, not cosmetic: eight of twenty-four courses differ, the entire marketing, market-research and econometrics block of Alternative 1 is absent, and Alternative 1's single sustainability course is replaced by a six-course sustainability and governance sequence.
traceOverrides: examines the institutional, political and cultural forces shaping global business and places cross-border governance and corporate responsibility at its centre, which is the responsibility question this programme is organised around

alternatives.label: Taking products and brands into unfamiliar markets: consumers, culture and communication
alternatives.concept: A question-led programme built on the target's own example of how a product can be introduced to consumers in an unfamiliar cultural market: it keeps the business, economics and research-methods foundations and the international operating environment, and then organises the programme around consumer behaviour and consumer psychology, marketing and market research, product development, the sociology of the societies in which markets are embedded, and the rhetoric and stylistics of persuasive communication. Its organising method is empirical and interpretive analysis of consumers and cultures rather than the administration of the firm.
alternatives.labelReason: The finished curriculum holds six marketing, consumer and product-development courses, three communication and rhetoric courses and four sociology courses next to a business, economics and methods foundation, so the label names the market-entry question and the consumer, cultural and communication material that answers it, rather than presenting the programme as a marketing degree.
progression: Entrepreneurship & Business Foundations, Introduction to Economics and Introduction to Sociology open semester one and Research Methods & Statistics follows in semester two, so both gateway courses precede every course that formally requires them. The Art of Rhetorical Communication in semester three precedes Persuasive Communication in semester five; Introduction to Sociology and Modern Sociology both precede New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory, which the course evidence states builds on them; Social Psychology precedes the consumer and marketing work of semesters four to six; and Research Methods & Statistics and Statistics & Experimental Methods precede Market Research and Qualitative Research Methodology. Every formal prerequisite is completed earlier and every course is available in its assigned term.
alternatives.distinctness: Alternative 1 administers the firm and Alternative 2 asks what the firm is responsible for; Alternative 3 asks how a product and a brand actually travel into a market whose culture the firm does not share. That question changes the curriculum rather than its label: nine of twenty-four courses differ from Alternative 1 and fourteen from Alternative 2. Accounting, finance, econometrics, sustainability and the whole leadership sequence give way to consumer product design, social psychology, behavioural economics, four sociology courses on how societies and modern market cultures are constituted, and three courses on rhetoric, stylistics and the ethics of persuasion, with market research and qualitative methodology retained as the empirical means of studying consumers.
traceOverrides: examines the contract, sales-of-goods, intellectual-property and digital-commerce rules that govern taking a product into another jurisdiction, and practises identifying the legal risk in exactly that kind of market entry
develops hands-on work with the kinds of data consumer research produces, including cleaning, manipulation, visualisation and text data, and requires an independent data-analysis project
integrates psychological evidence into economic theory and shows experimentally how biases, heuristics and framing shape the consumer choices that marketing has to anticipate

routeSelection.basis: The normalized target is the generic International Business Administration bachelor, and the adopted 2026-2027 programme schedule requires one of eleven year-3 specializations, each fixing two 6-EC courses and the subject of the 12-EC thesis, so one must be instantiated. The regulations define the programme as international business administration and state that it prepares students for a subsequent master's in Business Administration or Entrepreneurship; its compulsory core includes Organization Theory, International Strategy and Business Processes. Accounting, Economics, Finance, Financial Management, Marketing, Strategic Human Resource Management / Leadership and Change Management, Digital Business Innovation and Transport and Supply Chain Management each deepen one functional discipline, while Entrepreneurship and Management Consulting apply strategy to a particular setting. Strategy and Organization is the general-management specialization of business administration: both of its courses list the compulsory Organization Theory and International Strategy courses as recommended background, and Foundations of Strategic Management is also the shared first course of the Entrepreneurship and Management Consulting specializations. It therefore best represents the programme's broad business-administration identity. The choice was made from the official evidence alone and does not improve the UCR match: both specialization rows and the thesis remain without a UCR counterpart.

selection.assessment: Three UCR alternatives are defensible and the maximum was reached. Alternative 1 is the closest feasible response to the VU target: it rebuilds the business-administration core from UCR's Business & Entrepreneurship cluster but cannot reproduce the programme's supply-chain management, business mathematics or information-systems courses, its exchange semester or its thesis. Alternative 2 follows the target's own explicit commitment to sustainability, responsible decision-making and corporate social responsibility across cultures and turns it into a programme about what responsible conduct requires, differing from Alternative 1 in eight of twenty-four courses. Alternative 3 follows the target's own example of introducing a product to consumers in an unfamiliar cultural market and answers it with consumer behaviour, sociology of markets and persuasive communication, differing from Alternative 1 in nine courses and from Alternative 2 in fourteen. A fourth direction, leading and building trust in diverse and virtual international teams, was assessed: its evidence is already substantively carried by the closest-match core, which schedules Personal Leadership, Leadership & Diversity Management and Psychology of Organizations & Leadership, and no genuinely different 24-course curriculum follows from it, so it was not advanced as a fourth candidate. No alternative was manufactured to reach three.

blocks: Academic foundations, research methods and independent research

Both teach the core academic skills of selecting and critically analysing sources, articulating research questions and arguments and writing and presenting academically. The UCR course adds personal and civic development and community engagement, which the VU course does not.

Both teach the statistics a business student needs, from descriptive measures to inferential testing, together with the research design in which they are used. The UCR course combines methodology and statistics in one course rather than separating them.

Both teach the quantitative analysis used in empirical research on people, including regression, analysis of variance and further multivariate models. The UCR course is set in the health and behavioural sciences rather than in business.

Both teach qualitative research: design, data collection and management, interpretation of meaning and dissemination. The VU course applies this to business questions; the UCR course applies it to social processes.

Both require students to integrate evidence in a complete empirical research project: designing it, collecting and analysing data and reporting the result. The VU project is discipline-general, while the UCR course carries out that project as market research.

UCR offers no business mathematics course. Mathematical Methods exists in the Data Science & Intelligent Systems cluster but is not part of any of these three programmes, and no scheduled course teaches calculus, algebra or mathematical modelling for business, so the row stays blank rather than being filled with a statistics course.

The 12-EC bachelor's thesis, written on an international business topic within the Strategy and Organization specialization, has no counterpart among the 24 scheduled UCR courses: none of these programmes contains a thesis. Independent research appears instead as the standardized optional 15-EC comparison element shown alongside this component.
Firms, organisations and the people in them

Both concern managing people, and both treat cultural and individual difference as the central practical problem of doing so. The VU course builds that on psychological foundations, while the UCR course works from leadership theory and diversity management.

Both examine how organisations work: structure, culture, motivation, group dynamics, power and decision-making. The VU course approaches this as organisation theory, while the UCR course works from organisational psychology and behaviour, so it covers the behavioural half of the subject at 300 level rather than the theory of organisational design as such.

Both study how people think, feel and behave in the presence of others as the basis for understanding behaviour in organisations and markets. The VU course frames that material as people in business and society; the UCR course teaches it as social psychology and does not take the firm as its setting.

No scheduled UCR course teaches the design, management and improvement of business processes. Consumer Product Design covers one product-development process and Strategy & Digital Transformation covers business-model change, but neither addresses business-process management as a subject, so the row stays blank.

Both teach economic principles as the foundation of the programme, covering consumer and firm behaviour, market structure and the main macroeconomic aggregates. The VU course frames those principles for a global era, a framing the UCR programmes carry in International Macroeconomics.

Both teach accepted accounting theory and practice with an emphasis on reading and analysing financial statements and annual reports. The UCR course additionally covers corporate finance, which the VU programme places in a separate second-year Finance course.

Both teach financial decision-making: analysing financial data, assessing risk and making investment, budgeting and funding decisions. The UCR course is a 300-level case-based course that also covers money and banking.
Strategy, markets, consumers and the international business environment

Both teach strategy formation, from analysis and vision through to execution, and both examine how business models change. The VU course frames strategy internationally, while the UCR course frames it around digital transformation; the international dimension is carried separately by International Business & Governance.

Both study marketing strategy and what drives consumer behaviour and engagement with brands. The VU course foregrounds cultural difference across markets, while the UCR course foregrounds consumer psychology, brand strategy and digital and AI-driven marketing.

UCR teaches no supply-chain management. Life Cycle Analysis & Circular Economy and R3: Recycling, Recovery, Remediation examine material flows for their environmental impact, not the planning, sourcing and logistics of a global supply chain, so no scheduled UCR course is a sufficiently direct counterpart and the row stays blank.

Both establish what sustainability means and which planetary limits economic activity operates within, as a first-year foundation for later sustainability work. The VU course does so from a business perspective; the UCR gateway course does so from sustainability science.

Both are dedicated ethics courses that teach the main normative theories and then apply them to contested practical questions. The VU course applies them to business, while the UCR course applies them to equality, poverty, future generations and climate change.
Digital technology, data and AI in business

Both concern turning organisational data into usable information, and both require students to work hands-on with data and report a result. The VU course studies information systems as business infrastructure, while the UCR course teaches data cleaning, manipulation and visualisation; UCR does not teach enterprise information systems.
Electives, specialization and exchange in the external programme
Genuine restricted-choice space in the VU curriculum, preserved as such with its full 6 EC. It is not matched to a UCR course because no single option is instantiated.

Foundations of Strategic Management is the period-4 course of the instantiated Strategy and Organization specialization. It is not matched to a UCR course: Strategy & Digital Transformation, the only strategy course in these programmes, is already matched to the compulsory International Strategy course, and no other scheduled UCR course studies the debates of strategic management at this depth.

Strategic Management from a Practice Perspective is the period-5 course of the instantiated Strategy and Organization specialization. It is not matched to a UCR course: no further scheduled UCR course asks students to build a firm-level strategic plan from the position of a chief executive, so the row keeps its full 6 EC on the VU side and stays blank on the UCR side.

The mandatory 30-EC exchange semester has no counterpart in these UCR programmes. UCR students may study abroad, but no exchange component is part of the 180 EC reconstructed here, so the row keeps its full 30 EC on the VU side and stays blank on the UCR side.

notes.text: Both the VU programme and the UCR programmes include substantial study of international business, economics, finance, marketing and research methods. The International Business Administration programme additionally includes specialist work in global supply chain management, business mathematics, business information systems and a mandatory 30-EC exchange semester, and it ends with a specialization and a bachelor's thesis in one business discipline. UCR students can instead combine the international business and governance, economics, marketing, data science, sustainability and law courses shown here, but those specialist components are not offered at UCR and independent research appears only as an optional element.

The VU programme organises study around a fixed sequence of compulsory 6-EC business courses, two restricted-choice electives, a mandatory semester abroad and a chosen year-3 specialization with a thesis. At UCR, comparable subjects are distributed across individually chosen 7.5-EC courses in business and entrepreneurship, government and society, media, culture and communication, environment and sustainability, and data science, with four courses in each of six semesters. The UCR programmes therefore cover related territory through a different curricular structure rather than reproducing the external programme course by course.
